extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers / TV audience interested in entertainment news
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and considerations for whether a comedian's material is acceptable for broadcast and whether other performers choose to participate; covers network programming rules, performer conscience, and community harm concerns. Focused on televised variety/comedy shows and guest-hosted segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to programming standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Hosts and performers are expected not to 'violate programming standards' when appearing on network television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Networks (here NBC) require performers to follow internal standards; producers seek assurances from guest hosts (e.g., Lorne Michaels: Clay 'has given me his word' he will not violate programming standards). Violation can prompt finding replacement acts and controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of expletive‑laden or lewd routines on broadcast TV
rubrics_metrics.description: Material heavily laced with expletives, lewd poetry, or explicit sexual references is problematic for broadcasters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: MTV previously banned Andrew Dice Clay after a monologue 'laced with lewd poetry and references to fat women and sex.' Such content can trigger bans, refusals to participate, and program changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for performer conscience and principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Performers may refuse to participate if a host's material conflicts with their conscience or principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Nora Dunn and Sinead O'Connor boycotting SNL; O'Connor's spokeswoman: 'It would be nonsensical ... to expect a woman to perform songs about a woman's experiences after a monologue by Andrew Dice Clay.' Producer response may be to replace guests if defections occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of language that equates to or evokes sexual violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Offensive language that in context amounts to or evokes the 'language of rape' is singled out as unacceptable beyond mere profanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote from Dunn: 'This is not about dirty words. This is about the language of rape.' Indicates a threshold where sexualized insult becomes harmfully violent/abusive and crosses broadcasting/ethical lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use derogatory or dehumanizing language toward protected or identity groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Routines that demean groups (women, racial/ethnic groups, sexual minorities) are objectionable and may be labeled sexist, racist, or homophobic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes Clay's act 'has been called racist and homophobic as well as sexist.' Dunn illustrates scale of offensiveness: 'If you took the word `woman' in his routine and replaced it with `Jew,' I guarantee you that person would not be on Saturday Night Live.' Such comparisons highlight community standards about targeting protected groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context sensitivity — sequencing and pairing of material matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The acceptability of a performance can depend on what precedes it; context and sequencing influence whether content is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: O'Connor's refusal is premised on the idea that a woman's personal songs are inappropriate to follow a host's offensive monologue. Producers should consider the flow of the show when booking and sequencing acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate reputational and PR consequences of controversial bookings
rubrics_metrics.description: Booking or defending a controversial performer can lead to public defections, media criticism, and on-air disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Michaels said he was surprised by defections but applauded conscience-driven refusals; hosts and producers should weigh potential backlash (e.g., name-calling in interviews, bans by other outlets) when deciding bookings.
